items.title: Singh v District Court of NSW [2026] NSWCCA 180
items.short: Singh v District Court of NSW
items.citation: [2026] NSWCCA 180
items.significance: An acquitted man refused a costs certificate said the lack of an interpreter made the hearing unfair; the Court held an appeal, not judicial review, was the route and that no unfairness or power to reopen existed.
items.document: Cases/Crime/Singh v District Court of NSW [2026] NSWCCA 180 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Singh v District Court of NSW [2026] NSWCCA 180 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead: **Prabhjot Singh** was tried by a jury at Penrith (25 March–14 April 2025) and **acquitted of all three charges**. He applied for a **costs certificate** under the *Costs in Criminal Cases Act 1967* (NSW). At the hearing on **21 November 2025** there was **no interpreter**, and the application was dismissed; on **4 December 2025** the judge said he could not reopen it (*functus officio*). He pursued two routes, representing himself with a Punjabi interpreter: **judicial review** in the Court of Appeal and a **leave appeal** in the Court of Criminal Appeal. Both were dismissed on **5 November 2026**.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.5 / crime.3.1 (appeals, court jurisdiction)** — choosing the correct avenue: a statutory appeal, not judicial review, where it is equally effective.
- **crime.3.5 / crime.3.2 (legal representation, adversary system)** — a party is bound by the choices of their lawyers; limits on revisiting a finally determined application.
- **Balancing interests and discretion** — the high threshold protects the State's ability to prosecute, while an acquitted person bears heavy costs.
- **inv.1.6 (procedural fairness)** — an interpreter complaint rejected because it made no material difference.
items.caution: A **class case summary**; the acquittals are not questioned and this is a costs and procedure decision. The charges were sexual offences against a former wife — **no detail is given and none should be added**. The header and paras 11 and 13 name the respondents inconsistently, some pre-trial dates in the file conflict, and Ch 4 of the Criminal Appeal Act is listed but not discussed. The Court did not decide the position of an unrepresented party. Check the judgment before quoting paragraph numbers.

sections.What the Court decided:
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Should the Court entertain judicial review when leave to appeal under *Criminal Appeal Act 1912* s 5F(3) was available? | **No.** Relief is discretionary and ordinarily refused where there is an "alternative and equally effective remedy" (at [42]); *Barr v DPP*, *Quach v NCAT*, *Makowska* applied |
| Did the lack of an interpreter deny procedural fairness? | **No.** He had counsel and a solicitor and "is bound by the forensic decisions made by his legal representatives" (at [113]); his everyday English let him raise concerns |
| Was any error material? | **No.** Costs, hardship and police conduct do not go to whether prosecuting was reasonable (at [119]); it…
sections.The test for a costs certificate: Under ss 2 and 3(1)(a) a certificate may issue only if a **fully informed prosecutor would not have found it reasonable** to prosecute. The Director-General, not the court, fixes the amount if a certificate issues (s 4), so **hardship is not part of the s 3 test**. An acquittal alone is not enough.

Hamze, asks the Supreme Court to **permanently stay** his prosecution as an abuse of process, arguing
the AFP's role in his return from Türkiye was unlawful. The hearing opened before **Justice Edward

sections.Formal extradition versus what is allege:
| | Formal extradition | Zakaria's return (as alleged) |
|---|---|---|
| Legal basis | *Extradition Act 1988* (Cth) and the Australia–Turkey treaty | Turkish **deportation** of a foreigner allegedly on a false passport |
| Safeguards | Double criminality and speciality | Bypassed |
| Who acts | Government to government, AGD the central authority | AFP told Türkiye of the charges and supplied his passport |
| Challenge | The person can contest surrender | Removed **before his Turkish appeal was decided**; he says he asked for Iraq or a third country |
| Custody in transit | Officials of the two states | **Six Hart International contractors**, allegedly **$1.1 million** paid by the AFP to Skyt…
sections.Day one of the hearing (19 October 2026):
- **Mark Conroy**, who led a 2021 investigation into the Alameddine group, was shown emails from
  the Attorney-General's office warning that deportation could **jeopardise the prosecution**.
- **Robert Scheeres**, one of the contractors, said Zakaria was never handcuffed and free to go; the
  defence then showed images of him in **flexi cuffs** on the flight.
- The first take-off from Istanbul was aborted after a **bird strike**; the party sat on the tarmac for
  **four days**. The defence calls it a kidnapping and says the AFP kept NSW Police out of the loop.
- The AFP maintains its actions were lawful; its case had not yet been put. The 18 October report
  was that a key witness, an ex-so…
sections.Week one (to 24 October 2026):
- **Crown concession (22 October)**: the prosecutor accepted that Zakaria was **prohibited** from being
  deported while his Turkish appeal was pending. That concerns **Turkish law** — it does not concede
  what Australian officials **knew**, which is the question *Moti* makes decisive.
- The ABC named the two companies paid the **$1.1 million** as **Skytraders** (charter) and **Hart
  International** (escort); Hart's CEO said it has held AFP contracts for 26 years, including two
  other fugitive transfers (unverified).
- NSW Police said they only ever considered **lawful extradition** and learned of the contractor flight
  when Zakaria landed in Darwin.

sections.Week two (to 31 October 2026):
- Evidence from **three AFP officers** was partly **suppressed** under the *Court Suppression and Non-publication
  Orders Act 2010* (NSW) s 8 — so reporting of the AFP's side is necessarily incomplete: open justice against
  protecting operational material.
- The defence calls the contractor payments a "sham"; the AFP maintains it acted lawfully. Arrest warrants issued in
  December 2021 preceded the December 2023 deportation.
- In *Moti* the High Court said the focus is on what Australian officials **did or did not do**, not only collusion;
  whether the AFP **knew** the removal was unlawful may be decisive. *Moti* also held that AFP payments to the
  complainant and family were not an abu…

|---|---|---|
| Legal basis | *Extradition Act 1988* (Cth) and the Australia–Türkiye treaty; AGD the central authority | Turkish deportation; AFP-funded private escort |
| Safeguards | Double criminality and **speciality** (trial limited to the extradited offences) | Avoided — murder charges were laid after his return and were not on the December 2023 warrant list |
| Right to challenge | Contest in the requested country | Removed while his Turkish appeal was pending; the Crown concedes removal was prohibited |
| Transparency | Formal request on the record | Much AFP evidence suppressed; officers testify with protection against self-inc…

  material may have encouraged Turkish police to remove him, and said Türkiye had threatened to send him to Lebanon.
- **Lead contractor (5 November, ABC)** testified that **no contractor zip-tied** Zakaria on the flight. He said Turkish

sections.Rule of law reading (Year 11 summary):
The same hearing works as a **rule of law** example: government bound by law at home and abroad, set against a court's
duty to try serious charges. A stay would follow *Moti* only if Australian officials' **knowledge and conduct** are
established; Ierace J's 2025 finding of prima facie unlawfulness under Turkish law did not find that the AFP knew.
sections.The test, and why the 2025 ruling matter:
A permanent stay rests on the court's **inherent power** to prevent its process being abused: would
continuing bring the administration of justice into disrepute? The applicant carries a **heavy
onus**; stays are granted only in exceptional cases, weighed against the strong public interest in
trying serious charges.

items.citation: Evidence summary of a DFAT sanctions notice for the Foreign Minister (republished by Mirage News) and an ABC federal politics live blog, both 5 November 2026; Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011 (Cth); Autonomous Sanctions Regulations 2011 reg 6A(4)
items.significance: Australia used its 2021 Magnitsky-style law against the leaders of both sides of Sudan's war, setting unilateral sanctions against UN sanctions and ICC prosecution as ways of enforcing human rights.

items.document: Human Rights/HR - Australia Sudan Human Rights Sanctions Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead: On **5 November 2026** the Foreign Minister, Senator Penny Wong, announced sanctions on **four individuals and one entity** over alleged serious human rights violations in Sudan's war, which began on **15 April 2023** between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The individuals named are **Burhan, Dagalo, Al-Tijani Al-Tahir Karshoum and Hussein Barsham**; the entity is the **Al-Baraa Bin Malik Brigade**, an SAF-aligned Islamist militia. The individuals face financial sanctions and travel bans; the entity faces financial sanctions only. **These are executive listings, not findings of guilt.**

- **hr.2.9 (statute law)** — the Autonomous Sanctions Act and reg 6A as domestic law enforcing international norms.

1. The Minister must be satisfied the target was responsible for or complicit in serious violations of the right to life, freedom from torture or freedom from slavery.
2. Since the 2021 amending Act the Minister must obtain the **Attorney-General's written agreement** (reg 6A).
3. The Minister designates for financial sanctions and declares individuals for travel bans; names go on DFAT's Consolidated List.
4. Dealing with a designated person's assets without authorisation is an offence; declared persons cannot enter or remain in Australia.
5. Listed persons may apply in writing for revocation; a **class-based humanitarian permit** lets aid work continue.

items.title: Ministers back a 'digital detox' for screens and AI in schools (The Conversation, 5 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Jason M. Lodge, The Conversation, 5 November 2026, on the Education Ministers Meeting communique of 2 November 2026; UDHR art 26; ICESCR art 13; CRC arts 28–29; CRC General Comment No. 25 (2021)
items.significance: Education ministers agreed to restrict screens and generative AI in schools by soft law, showing how the right to education is reinterpreted for the digital age and left to states to implement.
core_labels: A contemporary issue illustrating the promotion and/or enforcement of human rights
items.document: Human Rights/HR - Digital Detox in Schools Screen and AI Limits Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead: At the **Education Ministers Meeting (EMM) on 2 November 2026** the Commonwealth, states and territories agreed that technology and AI in schools must be **evidence-based and purposeful** and restricted where they do not support learning and wellbeing. Education Minister Jason Clare had floated a "good digital detox" after **PISA 2025** showed record-low maths and reading scores. **Most decisions are commitments to introduce, trial or consider; states, territories and sectors decide implementation.**

- **hr.1.2 / hr.3.1** — the right to education developing from a declaration to child-specific digital standards; the summary includes a TEEACL exemplar anchored to the 2022 HSC question on how recognition of a human right has developed.
- **Soft law and federalism** — non-legal measures promoting rights, implemented state by state. Pairs with the NSW phone ban and the under-16 social media law as protective measures.

items.lead: New Zealand voted on **Saturday 7 November 2026**; the ABC analysis (published the day before) examines party policies on Te Tiriti. The National–ACT–NZ First coalition has already wound back Treaty-based provisions by **ordinary Acts passed on simple majorities**, because New Zealand has no entrenched constitution for these matters. Party pledges are campaign promises only.

sections.How a Waitangi Tribunal claim works: A permanent commission of inquiry (Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975), not a court: (1) a Maori person or group lodges a claim of a Crown breach; (2) claims are registered and grouped (new historical claims closed in 2008); (3) a panel hears claimants and the Crown; (4) it reports whether each claim is well-founded and recommends a remedy; (5) the Crown decides whether to act. Most recommendations are **non-binding**; binding powers over Crown forest licence and former state-owned enterprise land have never been fully used.
sections.Key facts:
- Maori ethnic group: 887,493 people (**17.8%**, 2023 Census); the "nearly one million" figure is Maori descent (978,246).
- A Human Rights Commission survey (Horizon, Dec 2025): **70%** of New Zealanders want Te Tiriti protected in law and the constitution.
- In December 2025 the UN CERD urged NZ to restore s 7AA and revitalise a Maori health authority, and warned against reinterpreting the Treaty without Maori free, prior and informed consent.
- Comparison: Australia's Voice referendum failed in October 2023 (60.06% No); Victoria passed its statewide Treaty Bill in October 2025.

items.significance: The UN Charter protects sovereign equality yet gives five permanent members a veto over enforcement, so a Ukraine veto, an ignored ICC warrant and US action in Venezuela test the post-1945 rules.

sections.Yalta-era bargaining v the Charter:
| | Yalta, Feb 1945 | UN Charter and later rules |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides | Big Three settle other nations' futures | Art 2(1): sovereign equality of all members |
| Territory and force | USSR promised a Manchurian sphere | Art 2(4): no threat or use of force against territorial integrity |
| Internal affairs | "Friendly" governments in Eastern Europe | Art 2(7): no UN intervention in domestic matters, except Chapter VII |
| Great-power privilege | A veto for each permanent member agreed | Art 27(3): the P5 can block enforcement against themselves |
| Protecting people | Pledge of free elections | R2P (2005): a political commitment, not a treaty |
sections.Why enforcement stalls when a permanent:
1. Russia began military operations in Ukraine on **24 February 2022**.
2. On **25 February 2022** Russia vetoed a Security Council draft condemning its aggression, despite **11 votes in favour (11–1–3)**.
3. The General Assembly passed ES-11/1 (**141 to 5**) demanding withdrawal, but it is **not binding**; since April 2022 every veto triggers an Assembly debate within 10 working days.
4. On 16 March 2022 the ICJ ordered Russia to suspend operations (13–2); the same day Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe, and it left the ECHR in September 2022.
5. The ICC issued warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova (17 March 2023); Russia, never a party to the Rome Statute, calls them meaningless,…

items.significance: Reddit and a libertarian group ask the High Court to strike down the under-16s social media ban, testing whether an implied freedom, not a bill of rights, can check a law protecting children.

items.lead: The first major legal challenge to the under-16s social media ban was heard in the High Court on **3 and 4 November 2026**. Australia has no guaranteed right to free speech, so both challengers rely on the **implied freedom of political communication**: they say stopping under-16s holding accounts burdens political communication, and the Commonwealth says the law serves a legitimate purpose, reducing harm from features such as algorithms, infinite scroll and notifications. **No decision has been made.**

items.significance: A UN expert invited to Australia was refused entry to two youth detention centres holding mostly First Nations children — the third UN access dispute since 2022.

items.lead:
The Special Rapporteur's official visit runs **2–13 November 2026**. The NT and Queensland refused planned visits to
**Holtze** and **Cleveland**, where about **97%** of children at Cleveland were Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander at
inspection. It is the second time in under a year the NT has blocked UN experts. First Nations young people are detained at **25.7 per 10,000** (2024–25), against a
Closing the Gap target of a 30% fall by 2031; the Productivity Commission assesses no change.

sections.What the mandate asks v what happened:
| UN terms of reference | November 2026 |
|---|---|
| Access to all places of detention | Holtze and Cleveland visits refused |

| Freedom of movement | Visit otherwise proceeding |

The terms of reference are UN guidelines, not a treaty: visits depend on the state's invitation and cooperation.

terms of reference, **not OPCAT**; cooperation rests on invitation. Preliminary findings are due in Sydney on **13
November 2026**.

items.lead:

  limits on what an order can achieve where no Convention applies.
- **fam.2.2 / fam.3.4** — a child's relationship with her mother and family as central to welfare; protection from

sections.The two gates to jurisdiction:
| | Gate 1 — citizenship | Gate 2 — habitual residence |

| Result | Met | Born and raised in NSW, at school here since kindergarten, family here; ties to Country B too weak to lose habitual residence |

  father, time with the mother as agreed; a **Child Impact Report** (s 62G) and reports from DCJ and NSW Police

items.title: Danby & Sorner [2026] FedCFamC1F 639
items.citation: [2026] FedCFamC1F 639
items.significance: After a mother's death, an aunt asks to move three children over their grandmother's undisclosed mental illness; the court keeps them in place and adds safeguards, because risk must be shown and stability matters.
core_labels: The roles of courts and dispute resolution methods
items.document: Cases/Family/Danby & Sorner [2026] FedCFamC1F 639 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Danby & Sorner [2026] FedCFamC1F 639 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Three children (two with health conditions) whose parents separated in April 2021. The children began living with
their mother in Sydney in September 2025; in 2026 **the mother died** and they lived with the paternal aunt. On
**1 July 2026** interim orders let them relocate to Victoria with the maternal grandmother and aunt. On **24 August
2026** the paternal aunt applied again after subpoenaed material showed the grandmother had a long-treated mental
illness she had not disclosed. Hearing 11 September; **orders and reasons 22 September 2026**. The father is
overseas. (Pseudonyms.)
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.3.4 / fam.2.2** — extended family stepping in after a parent's death; protection of vulnerable children from
  the risk of a carer's illness.
- **fam.2.5** — the court, the children's lawyer and a single expert managing a dispute through monitoring orders.
- **Compliance** — duties to disclose and report, backed by orders.
items.caution:
A **class-made summary of an interim judgment** (56 paragraphs); nothing here is a final decision. The summary lists
s 140(2) of the *Evidence Act 1995* (Cth) for the civil standard of proof. Check the quotes ([24], [39], [46], [48])
against the reasons before relying on them. Children and a parent's mental illness: keep non-graphic.

sections.Held:
- **Interim orders are "only a waypoint on the road to a final solution"** (at [24]).
- **Safety first, on evidence**: s 60CC puts safety first after the 2024 amendments, but a risk must be found on
  evidence, not assumed (*Barnabas & Phineus*; *Fitzwater*; *Isles & Nelissen*).
- **The non-disclosure**: the grandmother "should have known about the importance to the Court" of adequate
  information (at [39]), but her illness was long stable and treated, with no recent relapse.
- **Stability**: continuity of care is "integral to the safety and wellbeing" of the children (at [46]); the maternal
  aunt is, "in effect, a safety net" (at [48]).
sections.The orders:
| Safeguard | Detail |
|---|---|
| Treatment reports | Letters from the grandmother's psychologist on four set dates; she stays engaged with her psychiatrist and psychologist |
| Notice | Lawyers told within **24 hours** of any hospital admission; the aunt must remove the children if the grandmother deteriorates |
| Expert | A **single expert psychiatrist** to prepare a family report; costs shared 50/50 |
| Father | Electronic contact only |
| Not ordered | Moving the children to Sydney, or travel overseas |

Next case management: **26 October 2026**.

items.significance: A father's positive hair test, shortly after a haircut, kept his time supervised until two clear tests — the court gave weight to a single expert's untested opinion and refused leave for a second toxicologist.

items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Gittings & Gittings [2026] FedCFamC1F 648 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead: A mother and father of **two very young children** (pseudonyms) separated finally on 1 November 2024. By **consent orders of 18 December 2025** the father's time was supervised and he was to undergo urinalysis and hair-follicle testing. On 17 April 2026 Judge McGinn discharged supervision and restrained cutting of the father's hair; a **positive June 2026 test** was disclosed and supervision was reinstated by agreement. **Professor Christie** was appointed single toxicology expert by consent on 31 July 2026. The interim hearing was on 24 August 2026; judgment on **23 September 2026**.

- **Evidence in family proceedings** — the single expert policy, untested interim evidence, and weight versus admissibility.
- **Compliance** — conditions (testing, hair length) designed so compliance can be verified.

sections.The three questions and answers:

sections.Legal pathways for a remote young victim:

items.lead: Anglicare Australia tested **48,776 rental listings** (collected 14–15 March 2026) against the full-time adult award wage of **16 essential occupations**. "Affordable" means rent of no more than 30% of a single person's income. A nurse could afford **1.1%** of listings (558), a hospitality worker **0.7%** (338), and **no** listings were affordable for a hospitality worker in the NT. sections.Challenging an excessive rent increase i:
1. **Notice** — written notice of the new rent at least 60 days ahead; most tenancies allow one increase in any 12 months.
2. **Check validity** — an invalid notice need not be paid; an invalid increase already paid can be reclaimed at NCAT within 12 months.
3. **Apply to NCAT** — within 30 days of the notice, under *Residential Tenancies Act 2010* s 44.
4. **Tribunal** — compares rents for similar premises; it does **not** consider the tenant's income.

Because the test is market rent, s 44 protects against outliers, **not market-wide rises** like those in the report. NSW limits the *frequency* of increases and ended no-grounds evictions in May 2025, but sets no cap on the *amount*.

sections.Victoria v NSW:
| | Victoria (levy) | NSW (planning controls) |
|---|---|---|
| Law | *Short Stay Levy Act 2024*, from 1 January 2025 | SEPP (Housing) 2021, framework from 1 November 2021 |
| Mechanism | **7.5%** of booking fees for stays under 28 days, earmarked for housing | Mandatory register, code of conduct; 180-day cap on non-hosted stays in some areas |
| Who pays | Booking platform, or the owner for direct bookings | Host registers; $65 first-year fee |
| Housing revenue | Yes | None |

The Government, Opposition, Greens and industry responded; NSW announced a short-term rental review in December 2023.
sections.The land tax package, and how the figure:

items.title: Antakirinja Matu-Yankunytjatjara Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC v State of South Australia [2026] FCA 1663
items.significance: A native title body's narrow variation of a 2011 consent determination proceeds, but a self-represented respondent cannot use it to reopen who the native title holders are.
core_labels: Overview of native title — overturning terra nullius and the relationship to land rights
Outcomes of change to native title law — benefits and limitations
items.document: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Antakirinja Matu-Yankunytjatjara Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC v State of South Australia [2026] FCA 1663 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead: The **Antakirinja Matu-Yankunytjatjara (AMY)** native title body (AMYAC, the prescribed body corporate) applied under **s 61 of the *Native Title Act 1993* (Cth)** to vary the **11 May 2011** consent determination (*Lennon v State of South Australia* [2011] FCA 474) in **four limited ways**. A respondent, **Ms Brown**, who appeared for herself, asked for leave to issue subpoenas and sought to raise the description of who the native title holders are. The hearing was on 4 November 2026; reasons were published on **5 November 2026**.
items.use_it_for:
- **chg.5.2 / chg.5.5 (native title overview and outcomes)** — a determination is a living order that courts vary as law develops (here, after *Brown*), and a limit: disputes about *who holds* title cannot be reopened through a variation.
- **chg.5.4** — a later judicial decision feeding into variation of a determination.
- **inv.2.3** — holder identity ties Country, people and kinship (birth, association, descent).
- **Procedural fairness** — a self-represented respondent was heard but her requests failed on relevance.
items.caution: A **Year 11 class summary** of a short procedural judgment; there is **no HSC edition**. The merits of Ms Brown's claim were **not decided** — do not suggest she is wrong about her own ancestry. *Western Australia v Brown* is unrelated to Ms Brown. The case concerns Aboriginal group identity and family membership: handle respectfully. Check quotations ([20], [21], [23], [24]) against the judgment.

sections.What the applicant asked to change:
1. Delete two paragraphs that assumed no native title in pastoral improvements, after *Western Australia v Brown* (2014) 253 CLR 507.
2. Add land parcels to the extinguishment schedules (to help compensation).
3. Add parcels to the surrender schedules (under an agreement).
4. A correction to the determination.

The 2011 **description of the native title holders** was **not** touched.
sections.Held — O'Bryan J, 5 November 2026:
| Issue | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Does the variation put the description of the holders in issue? | **No** — "AMYAC does not seek to vary that description" (at [20]) |
| Can a respondent apply to vary that description? | **No** — a respondent "has no entitlement to apply to vary the description of the native title holders" (at [21]) |
| Do the proposed subpoenas have a legitimate forensic purpose? | **No** — the documents "are not relevant to the issues that arise in the proceeding" (at [24]) |

sections.Authorities: *Lennon* [2011] FCA 474 (the determination being varied); *Western Australia v Brown* (2014) 253 CLR 507 (native title can exist in pastoral improvements); *Seven Network v Fairfax Media* [2023] FCAFC 185 and *Wong v Sklavos* [2014] FCAFC 120 (a subpoena needs a legitimate forensic purpose).
